title: Stokes Theorem and Applications
short_intro: Stokes' Theorem relates the surface integral of the curl of a vector field over an open surface to the line integral of the vector field around the boundary curve of that surface. It forms a fundamental bridge between differential vector calculus and integral theorems in classical mechanics and electromagnetism.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Evaluation of simple line integrals and curl calculations in Cartesian coordinates.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Application of Stokes' theorem to verify conservative force fields, central force potentials, and hydrodynamic circulations.

prerequisites: Vector differentiation and concept of gradient, divergence, and curl
Line integrals and surface integrals of vector fields

concept_notes.heading: Statement of Stokes' Theorem
bullets: Let S be a piecewise smooth, oriented open surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise smooth boundary curve C.
If vector field F has continuous first-order partial derivatives in a domain containing S, then the line integral of F along C equals the surface integral of the curl of F over S.
The orientation of curve C and surface S must follow the right-hand screw rule.

concept_notes.heading: Physical Interpretation of Curl
bullets: The curl of a vector field represents the infinitesimal rotation or vorticity of the field at a point.
If velocity field v of a fluid has non-zero curl, the fluid flow exhibits local rotation.
In mechanics, if a force field F satisfies curl F = 0 everywhere, the field is irrotational and conservative.

concept_notes.heading: Path Independence and Conservative Fields
bullets: For a conservative force field (such as a central gravitational force), the line integral around any closed loop is identically zero.
By Stokes' theorem, this implies that curl F = 0 for a conservative force field.
Potential energy V can be defined such that F = -\nabla V.

concept_notes.heading: Geometrical Conditions and Boundary Orientation
bullets: The surface S must be two-sided with a defined unit normal vector n^.
The direction of integration along the boundary curve C is chosen such that if you walk along C with your head pointing in the direction of n^, the surface S is always to your left.
Discontinuities in the vector field or its derivatives across the surface invalidate the theorem.

derivations.title: Proof of Stokes' Theorem for Infinitesimal Rectangular Loop
derivations.conditions: Vector field F with continuous partial derivatives in a region containing a differential rectangular element in the xy-plane.
steps: Consider a small rectangle in the xy-plane with sides dx and dy, centered at (x, y).
Calculate the line integral of F = F_x i^ + F_y j^ counterclockwise around the four sides of the rectangle.
Along the bottom side: F_x dx; along the right side: F_y dy + (\partial F_y / \partial x) dx dy; along the top side: -[F_x + (\partial F_x / \partial y) dy] dx; along the left side: -F_y dy.
Summing these contributions yields (\partial F_y / \partial x - \partial F_x / \partial y) dx dy.
Recognize the term in parentheses as the z-component of curl F, and dx dy as the differential surface area ds_z.

derivations.title: Equivalency of Line Integral to Circulation in Fluid Dynamics
derivations.conditions: Velocity field v of a fluid moving in a steady-state regime across an arbitrary bounded surface S.
steps: Define circulation \Gamma as the line integral of fluid velocity v around a closed material loop C.
Apply Stokes' theorem to convert the closed line integral of velocity into an open surface integral.
Substitute the curl of velocity, which equals twice the local angular velocity vector \omega (vorticity vector), into the surface integral.
Express circulation as the flux of vorticity through the surface bounded by the loop.
derivations.result: \Gamma = \oint_C v \cdot dr = \int_S (\nabla \times v) \cdot n^ ds = 2 \int_S \omega \cdot n^ ds

formula_sheet.equation_html: \nabla \times F = \left(\frac{\partial F_z}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial z}\right)i^ + \left(\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial x}\right)j^ + \left(\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}\right)k^

formula_sheet.conditions: Cartesian coordinate system with continuous first derivatives

formula_sheet.name: Stokes' Theorem in Component Form (z-normal)

formula_sheet.conditions: Surface lies entirely in the xy-plane

solved_numericals.question: Evaluate the line integral \oint_C (y i^ + x j^) \cdot dr where C is the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 in the xy-plane, oriented counterclockwise.
solution_steps: Identify the vector field F = y i^ + x j^ and curve C.
Method 1 (Direct integration): Parametrize circle as x = \cos \theta, y = \sin \theta, dx = -\sin \theta d\theta, dy = \cos \theta d\theta for \theta from 0 to 2\pi.

Substitute into line integral: \int_0^{2\pi} [(\sin \theta)(-\sin \theta) + (\cos \theta)(\cos \theta)] d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} \cos(2\theta) d\theta = 0.
Method 2 (Stokes' theorem): Calculate curl F = (\partial / \partial x(x) - \partial / \partial y(y)) k^ = (1 - 1) k^ = 0.
Since curl F = 0, the surface integral over S is zero.

solved_numericals.question: Verify Stokes' theorem for the vector field F = -y^3 i^ + x^3 j^ - z^3 k^ over the hemisphere S: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = R^2, z \ge 0, bounded by the circle x^2 + y^2 = R^2 in the xy-plane.
solution_steps: Boundary curve C is x = R \cos \theta, y = R \sin \theta, z = 0, with dr = (-R \sin \theta i^ + R \cos \theta j^) d\theta.
Line integral: \oint_C F \cdot dr = \int_0^{2\pi} [(-R^3 \sin^3 \theta)(-R \sin \theta) + (R^3 \cos^3 \theta)(R \cos \theta)] d\theta = R^4 \int_0^{2\pi} (\sin^4 \theta + \cos^4 \theta) d\theta.
Evaluating the integral gives R^4 (3\pi/4 + 3\pi/4) = 3\pi R^4 / 2.
Calculate curl F = \nabla \times F = 3x^2 k^ - (-3y^2 k^?) wait, recalculate: \nabla \times F = (0)i^ + (0)j^ + (3x^2 - (-3y^2))k^ = 3(x^2 + y^2)k^.
Surface integral: \int_S (3(x^2+y^2) k^) \cdot n^ ds. For the hemisphere, n^ ds = (x i^ + y j^ + z k^)/R ds_projected or integrate in spherical polar coordinates.
Using polar coordinates on xy plane projection: 3 \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^R (r^2) r dr d\theta = 3 \cdot (2\pi) \cdot [r^4/4]_0^R = \frac{3\pi R^4}{2}.
solved_numericals.answer: 3\pi R^4 / 2 (Both line and surface integrals match)

solved_numericals.question: A force field is given by F = (2x + y^2) i^ + (3y - 4x) j^. Find the work done in moving a particle once counterclockwise around the triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0), and (0,1) using Stokes' theorem.
solution_steps: Use Stokes' theorem: W = \oint_C F \cdot dr = \iint_S (\nabla \times F) \cdot k^ dx dy.
Calculate curl F_z = \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(3y - 4x) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2x + y^2) = -4 - 2y.
Set up the double integral over the triangular region S bounded by x = 0, y = 0, and x + y = 1.

assumptions_and_limitations: The vector field must possess continuous first-order partial derivatives throughout the region containing the surface and its boundary.
The surface S must be orientable; non-orientable surfaces such as a Möbius strip cannot be analyzed with standard Stokes' theorem.
The boundary curve C must be a simple closed curve without self-intersections.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Stokes' theorem requires the surface to be flat (planar).
common_misconceptions.correct: Stokes' theorem applies to any smooth or piecewise smooth open 3D surface, provided it shares the same boundary curve C.
common_misconceptions.why: The surface integral evaluates the curl flux through any arbitrary open surface spanning the boundary.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The orientation of the curve C can be chosen arbitrarily without matching the surface normal.
common_misconceptions.correct: The direction of curve integration and surface normal must strictly follow the right-hand screw rule.
common_misconceptions.why: Failing to respect orientation results in a sign error in the calculated integral.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If curl F = 0 at a single point, the line integral around any closed loop is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: The curl must be zero everywhere in a simply connected domain for the line integral around any closed loop to vanish.
common_misconceptions.why: Zero curl at an isolated point does not guarantee irrotationality across the entire enclosed surface.

quick_revision: Stokes' theorem connects an open surface integral of curl F to a closed line integral of F.
Formula: \oint_C F \cdot dr = \int_S (\nabla \times F) \cdot n^ ds.
If \nabla \times F = 0, the force field is conservative and irrotational.
Right-hand rule governs the relationship between the boundary curve direction and surface normal.
